XIX.1.title: Zizhang on the shi
XIX.1.reflection: Book XIX gives no sayings of the Master; it records the disciples. Zizhang begins: the shi gives his life in danger, thinks of rightness before gain, of reverence at sacrifice, of grief in mourning. That is enough. It is close to XIV.13, in a disciple's own words.
XIX.1.question: Which of the four comes most naturally to you?

XIX.2.title: Neither here nor there
XIX.2.reflection: Holding to virtue without enlarging it, believing in the Way without conviction: can such a person be said to exist, or not to? A half-hearted virtue counts for neither presence nor absence.
XIX.2.question: What do you hold half-heartedly?

XIX.3.title: Whom to befriend
XIX.3.reflection: Zixia's students ask Zizhang about friendship. Zixia says: befriend those who are worthy, refuse those who are not. Zizhang disagrees: the junzi honours the worthy and tolerates everyone, praises the good and pities the unable. If I am worthy, whom can I not tolerate? If not, others will refuse me; how could I refuse them? Two disciples, two schools.
XIX.3.question: Do you choose friends by Zixia's rule or Zizhang's?

XIX.4.title: Lesser ways
XIX.4.reflection: Zixia: even small arts have something worth seeing, but pursued too far they mire one; so the junzi does not make them his work. A specialist skill, valuable, is not the whole of a life.
XIX.4.question: What small art could take more of your life than it deserves?

XIX.5.title: Each day, each month
XIX.5.reflection: Zixia: to learn each day what one did not know, and each month not forget what one has mastered, may be called loving learning. The definition is a rhythm of days and months.
XIX.5.question: What did you learn today, and what are you keeping from last month?
XIX.5.exercise: Tonight write down one thing you did not know this morning.

XIX.6.title: Ren is in it
XIX.6.reflection: Zixia: study widely and hold firmly to your aim, ask earnestly and reflect on what is near; ren is in this. Learning and goodness are not separate.
XIX.6.question: What near question could you reflect on today?

XIX.7.title: The workshop
XIX.7.reflection: Zixia: craftsmen stay in their workshops to perfect their work; the junzi learns to reach his Way. Learning is the junzi's workshop.
XIX.7.question: Where is your workshop?

XIX.8.title: Covering a fault
XIX.8.reflection: Zixia: the small man is sure to dress up his faults. Eight words that need no commentary.
XIX.8.question: What fault have you recently dressed up?

XIX.9.title: Three changes
XIX.9.reflection: Zixia: the junzi seems to change three times: from afar stern, close up mild, in speech exacting. A portrait close to VII.37.
XIX.9.question: How do you seem from afar, and close up?

XIX.10.title: Trust first
XIX.10.reflection: Zixia: the junzi wins trust before he burdens the people, or they will feel oppressed; wins his ruler's trust before he objects, or the ruler will feel slandered. The same words land differently depending on whether trust is there.
XIX.10.question: Whose trust do you need before you can tell them a hard truth?

XIX.11.title: Great and small virtues
XIX.11.reflection: Zixia: in great virtues do not cross the line; in small ones there is some room. Legge renders the image as a boundary passed and repassed. It is the most permissive line in the book, and it limits itself to small things.
XIX.11.question: Where is there room in your small virtues, and none in the great?

XIX.12.title: Sweeping and answering
XIX.12.reflection: Ziyou mocks Zixia's students: they can sprinkle, sweep, answer and bow, but these are branches; where is the root? Zixia answers: in the junzi's Way, what is taught first and what later? As plants differ, so do students. Only the sage holds beginning and end together. A real argument about teaching, recorded with both sides.
XIX.12.question: Do you learn better from the root or from the branches?

XIX.13.title: Office and learning
XIX.13.reflection: Zixia: when office leaves time, learn; when learning leaves time, take office. The two are meant to alternate through a life.
XIX.13.question: What could you learn in the spare time your work leaves?

XIX.14.title: Grief, and its end
XIX.14.reflection: Ziyou: mourning goes as far as grief, and stops there. Against displays of mourning beyond real feeling, and against grief made into a ritual of its own.
XIX.14.question: Is there a grief you are keeping beyond its end?

XIX.15.title: My friend Zizhang
XIX.15.reflection: Ziyou: my friend Zizhang does what is hard, but he is not yet ren. Admiration and a reservation in one line.
XIX.15.question: Whom do you admire with a reservation, and do they know it?

XIX.16.title: Hard to be ren beside him
XIX.16.reflection: Master Zeng: how imposing Zizhang is; it is hard to practise ren alongside him. Two disciples make the same judgement in two chapters, which says something about Zizhang and something about the circle.
XIX.16.question: With whom is it hard to be good, because they fill the room?

XIX.17.title: What mourning reveals
XIX.17.reflection: Master Zeng heard from the Master: people may not show all they have in them, except, surely, in mourning a parent. Grief brings out what ordinary days hide.
XIX.17.question: What did a loss reveal in you that you had not known?

XIX.18.title: Not changing his father's men
XIX.18.reflection: Master Zeng heard: the filial piety of Meng Zhuangzi was ordinary in most things, but in not changing his father's ministers and policies it was hard to equal. The rule of I.11, shown in a real man.
XIX.18.question: What did you keep of someone else's work after it passed to you?

XIX.19.title: Pity, not pride
XIX.19.reflection: The Meng family appoints Yang Fu as a judge, and he asks Master Zeng's advice. Those above have lost the Way and the people have long been scattered. When you uncover the facts of a crime, feel sorrow and pity, not pleasure in your skill. A judge is told to remember why people fall.
XIX.19.question: When you are right about someone's fault, what do you feel?

XIX.20.title: Downstream
XIX.20.reflection: Zigong: the tyrant Zhou was not so wicked as his name; so the junzi hates to live downstream, where all the world's filth flows to him. A bad reputation attracts every evil, deserved or not.
XIX.20.question: Whose bad name has collected more than their real faults?

XIX.21.title: Like an eclipse
XIX.21.reflection: Zigong: the faults of the junzi are like eclipses of the sun and moon: when he errs, everyone sees; when he corrects, everyone looks up. Visible faults and visible correction.
XIX.21.question: Who saw your last correction?

XIX.22.title: From whom did he learn?
XIX.22.reflection: Gongsun Chao asks from whom Zhongni, Confucius, learned. The Way of Wen and Wu has not fallen to the ground; it is in people, the worthy remembering the great parts and others the small. Where could the Master not learn? Why should he need a single teacher? The last books turn to defending the Master's reputation.
XIX.22.question: From how many teachers did you learn what you know best?

XIX.23.title: The wall and the house
XIX.23.reflection: A noble of Lu says Zigong is worthier than Confucius. Zigong uses an image: my wall is shoulder high, and anyone can look over and see the rooms; the Master's wall is many fathoms high, and without finding the gate one cannot see the temple's beauty. Few find the gate.
XIX.23.question: Whose depth did you miss because you did not find their gate?

XIX.24.title: Sun and moon
XIX.24.reflection: When the same noble disparages Confucius, Zigong answers: others' worth is a hill that can be climbed over; Zhongni is the sun and moon, which cannot. A man may cut himself off, but what harm does it do the sun and moon? It only shows he does not know his measure.
XIX.24.question: Whom have you dismissed who might be beyond your measure?

XIX.25.title: No stairs to Heaven
XIX.25.reflection: Chen Ziqin tells Zigong he is too modest: how is Confucius better than you? One word can make a man wise or foolish; be careful. The Master cannot be equalled, as Heaven cannot be climbed by a stair. If he had ruled a state, the people would have stood, followed and been at peace; living, honoured, dead, mourned. Zigong's last defence of his teacher.
XIX.25.question: Whom do you defend when they are not there to answer?
